newsitem.title: KUWAIT: Kuwaitis fear election will trigger sectarian row.
newsitem.headline: Kuwaitis fear election will trigger sectarian row.

text.p: Some Kuwaitis fear rivalry in the only direct parliamentary election on the Arab side of the Gulf could revive religious differences which they hoped had faded for good after the 1991 Gulf War, analysts said on Thursday.

Differences between some Sunni Moslems and members of the Shi'ite sect -- more than 25 percent of the oil state's 700,000 nationals -- emerged in the campaign for 50 parliamentary seats being contested on Monday in the second election since the war.
"We have returned to the splits," said economist Jasem al-Saadoun, speaking about a rift which many Kuwaitis believed was healed by the Gulf crisis after decades of mutual Sunni-Shi'ite suspicion.

"After the Gulf War this file was closed...Now people are talking about threats from within, not only the external threat (Iraq)," a liberal Shi'ite candidate who asked not to identified told Reuters.
Many Kuwaiti Sunnis were suspicious of their religious rivals during Iraq's 1980-88 war with Shi'ite Iran, in which Kuwait and most Arab states backed Baghdad, residents said.
Although many analysts expected the bitter sectarian exchanges gradually to fade away after the election, they feared the issue could linger on for some time to come.
"National unity is collapsing under the shovels of sectarian ideas (while) the government is watching...," Liberal Shi'ite deputy Ali al-Baghli, a former oil minister, told Reuters.

Crown Prince Sheikh Saad al-Abdulla al-Sabah told parliament in late 1995: "Safeguarding national unity...will always remain the wall which protects the sovereignty, dignity and achievements of the Kuwait people."
Politicians and newspapers alike urge Kuwaitis almost daily to abandon sectarian ideas and shun candidates trying to secure votes by using the issue in campaign rallies.
But a few members of the two main sects of Islam are trading accusations not heard since Iraq's 1990 invasion.
A few Shi'ite candidates have been accused by some ordinary Kuwaiti citizens and political opponents of close links with non-Arab Iran, which is ruled by Shi'ite clergymen.

Sunni lawyer Mohammad al-Jasem, during a rally for a Sunni candidate at which a leading traditionalist Shi'ite MP was present, even accused Shi'ite candidates of contacts with Iranian intelligence. Al-Watan newspaper highlighted his remarks.
Liberal Sunni MP Ahmad al-Rubai said: "There are people who are tickling sentiments of sectarianism...for a seat even if the nation is the victim.
"With this diversity there is only one solution. We have to feed tolerance to our children," he told a rally by fellow university professor Abdul-Rida Asiri, a Shi'ite.

Political parties are not permitted in Kuwait -- a rule aimed at avoiding upsetting a delicate social balance which also includes nationals with more rights than others, tribal powers, stateless Arabs and influential trading families.
Only 107,000 Kuwaiti men born to Kuwaiti fathers are eligible to vote. Military and police personnel, Kuwaitis naturalised less than 20 years ago, citizens under 21 and women cannot vote.
